A1-A2.headline: The Long History of People Who Trade Goods

pages.text:
Picture a busy old market full of warm smells and bright goods. Sellers link the people who make things with the people who buy them.

From old shops to modern online stores, sellers have always helped business grow.
pages.caption: Merchants in a Southern Port

evidence.fileTitle: File:Merchants in a Southern Port by Thomas Wyck c1660.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Merchants in a Southern Port by Thomas Wyck c. 1660

pages.text:
The Phoenicians were among the most famous business people in early history. By the 9th century BCE, they led sea trade across the Mediterranean.

They sold wood, cloth, and bright purple dye, and shared a clear alphabet.
pages.caption: Phoenician traders across the Mediterranean region

imageProvenance.imageAttribution: Publisher New York Ward, Lock (Public domain)

evidence.articleCaption: Phoenician merchants traded across the entire Mediterranean region

pages.text:
Social rank for business people differed by place. In Rome, farming held more honor, yet some sellers grew very rich, like Umbricius Scaurus with his fine fish sauce.

Roman goods even reached southern China by 226 CE.
pages.caption: Mosaic showing a garum container from Pompeii

evidence.articleCaption: Mosaic showing garum container, from the house of Umbricius Scaurus of Pompeii. The inscription which reads "G(ari) F(los) SCO(mbri) SCAURI EX OFFI(CI)NA SCAURI" has been translated as "The flower of garum, made of the mackerel, a product of Scaurus, from the shop of Scaurus"

pages.text:
The word merchant comes from an old Latin word for buying and selling. By the 16th century, many artists painted rich shop owners and their groups.

Those pictures show how trading families grew strong across Europe.
pages.caption: Costumes of merchants from Brabant and Antwerp

evidence.fileTitle: File:16th century costumes of merchants from Brabant and Antwerp.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Costumes of merchants from Brabant and Antwerp, engraving by Abraham de Bruyn, 1577

glossary.en_def: a person who buys and sells goods
the activity of buying and selling

B1-B2.headline: From Ancient Markets to Global Trade Networks

pages.text:
Picture a lively ancient market filled with rich scents and goods. Merchants link producers to buyers across local stalls and global networks.

From ancient streets to modern online platforms, they have always driven growth.
pages.caption: Merchants in a Southern Port

evidence.fileTitle: File:Merchants in a Southern Port by Thomas Wyck c1660.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Merchants in a Southern Port by Thomas Wyck c. 1660

pages.text:
The Phoenicians ranked among history's most influential traders. By the 9th century BCE, they led commerce across the Mediterranean.

They exported wood, cloth, and prized purple dye while spreading a practical alphabet.
pages.caption: Phoenician traders across the Mediterranean region

imageProvenance.imageAttribution: Publisher New York Ward, Lock (Public domain)

evidence.articleCaption: Phoenician merchants traded across the entire Mediterranean region

pages.text:
Merchants held uneven social standing across eras. In Rome, trade ranked below farming, yet figures like Umbricius Scaurus grew wealthy selling fine fish sauce.

Vast Roman trade even reached southern China by 226 CE.
pages.caption: Mosaic showing a Roman fish sauce jar

evidence.articleCaption: Mosaic showing garum container, from the house of Umbricius Scaurus of Pompeii. The inscription which reads "G(ari) F(los) SCO(mbri) SCAURI EX OFFI(CI)NA SCAURI" has been translated as "The flower of garum, made of the mackerel, a product of Scaurus, from the shop of Scaurus"

pages.text:
The word merchant stems from the Latin term for trading. By the 16th century, European painters often chose merchants and trade guilds as subjects.

These portraits reveal their rising power in shaping modern economies.
pages.caption: Costumes of merchants from Brabant and Antwerp

evidence.fileTitle: File:16th century costumes of merchants from Brabant and Antwerp.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Costumes of merchants from Brabant and Antwerp, engraving by Abraham de Bruyn, 1577

having a great influence on someone or something

C1-C2.headline: The Enduring Legacy of the Mercantile Class

pages.text:
Envision a vibrant ancient bazaar brimming with distant commodities. Merchants mediate between producers and consumers across regional markets and global networks.

From antiquity to digital commerce, they have propelled prosperity.
pages.caption: Merchants in a Southern Port by Thomas Wyck

evidence.fileTitle: File:Merchants in a Southern Port by Thomas Wyck c1660.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Merchants in a Southern Port by Thomas Wyck c. 1660

pages.text:
Among antiquity's preeminent commercial peoples, the Phoenicians dominated Mediterranean exchange by the 9th century BCE.

Exporting timber, textiles, and prized Tyrian purple dye, they disseminated an efficient alphabet across the region.
pages.caption: Phoenician traders across the Mediterranean region

imageProvenance.imageAttribution: Publisher New York Ward, Lock (Public domain)

evidence.articleCaption: Phoenician merchants traded across the entire Mediterranean region

pages.text:
Mercantile prestige fluctuated markedly across civilizations. Though Roman elites privileged agriculture, entrepreneurs like Umbricius Scaurus prospered via artisanal fish sauce.

Roman commercial networks even reached southern China by 226 CE.
pages.caption: Mosaic showing a garum container from Pompeii

evidence.articleCaption: Mosaic showing garum container, from the house of Umbricius Scaurus of Pompeii. The inscription which reads "G(ari) F(los) SCO(mbri) SCAURI EX OFFI(CI)NA SCAURI" has been translated as "The flower of garum, made of the mackerel, a product of Scaurus, from the shop of Scaurus"

pages.text:
Derived from Latin commercial terminology, the merchant emerged as a prominent pictorial subject by the 16th century.

Individual portraits and guild canvases chronicled ascending mercantile power across evolving European economies.
pages.caption: Costumes of merchants from Brabant and Antwerp

evidence.articleCaption: Costumes of merchants from Brabant and Antwerp, engraving by Abraham de Bruyn, 1577
